summary: Arabic has singular, dual and plural. Plurals are sound (masculine -ūna/-īna, mostly for male humans; feminine -ātun) or broken (a new vowel pattern, كِتَاب → كُتُب). Most vegetables are collective nouns: the collective (جَزَر “carrots” as food or in general) is grammatically masculine singular; one piece is the unit noun in -a (جَزَرَة “a carrot”); counted pieces take the sound feminine plural -āt (جَزَرَات). Mass nouns without a unit noun (طَمَاطِم، سَبَانِخ، ذُرَة) are counted with حَبَّة “a piece” or رَأْس “a head”. Non-human plurals take feminine singular agreement: هٰذِهِ جَزَرَاتٌ (these are carrots).

askYourself: Do I mean the vegetable in general or as food (→ collective, no plural needed) or counted pieces (→ unit noun, then -āt)?
Is it a sound feminine plural in -āt? → accusative and genitive both end in -i (-ātin / -āti), never -a.
Is the plural non-human? → feminine singular agreement: هٰذِهِ (not هٰؤُلَاءِ), هِيَ (not هُمْ).
Is there a unit noun at all? If not, count with حَبَّةُ … or رَأْسُ …

traps: Sound feminine plural: الْجَزَرَاتِ in the accusative (with -i), not *الْجَزَرَاتَ.
Non-human plurals are “she”: الْبَصَلَاتُ؟ هِيَ هُنَا.
A collective is singular: الْبَصَلُ رَخِيصٌ (onions are cheap).
From 3 to 10 the number takes the opposite gender and the counted noun is a genitive plural: ثَلَاثُ جَزَرَاتٍ.
